title: Nepal seeks US$20m from UN loss-and-damage fund for the devastating Bhotekoshi floods - Asia Insurance Review
description: Nepal seeks US$20m from UN loss-and-damage fund for the devastating Bhotekoshi floods  Asia Insurance Review
publisher.title: Asia Insurance Review
full_article:
Currently the total economic losses due to the catastrophic floods have been put at $2.7bn. More than 1,400 people were killed and thousands were left unaccounted for after flash floods struck Nepal.

According to a report by Yahoo Finance, the UN Loss-and-Damage Fund was established in 2023. Between December 2025 and July 2026, the Fund received 176 applications seeking more than $2.8bn. However, as of September 2026, no country had received any money from the fund. The Fund allows a maximum of $20m as financial compensation for any one country for a single CAT event.

Nepal's disaster management authority estimated about $2.7bn in physical damage and economic losses from the floods. Add another $4.8bn in recovery and reconstruction costs, and the country's $20m request looks even smaller against its overall need.

title: Nepal’s three main crossings with China disrupted by monsoons — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal’s three main crossings with China disrupted by monsoons — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal has experienced simultaneous disruptions at three main land crossings on its border with China — Korala, Rasuwagadhi-Kerung and Tatopani. This has complicated trade and cargo transportation ahead of Dashain, the country’s largest Hindu festival, Kathmandu Post reports.

Landslides cut off the route to Korala

The Korala crossing in Mustang District was the latest to face disruptions. Three days of heavy rain caused floods, landslides and road washouts along the Beni-Jomsom section of the Kali Gandaki corridor. According to local authorities, more than 50 landslides occurred on the Maldhunga-Beni-Jomsom highway in Parbat District.

Flooding also washed away part of the road leading to the bridge over the Kali Gandaki River in Pokharabagar, leaving the northern part of Myagdi District and all of Mustang without road access. Tejaswi Sharma, head of the transport corridor project, said clearing landslides in Mustang and Parbat could take up to three days, while restoring the bridge and clearing major landslides could take up to a week.

More than 200 containers are stranded at the customs yard in Korala. Before the bad weather, around 50 containers were processed there daily. According to traders, the cargo includes festival goods, essential items and other commercial products.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Other crossings are also not operating

The Rasuwagadhi-Kerung crossing has been unusable since flooding on August 26 damaged roads and infrastructure. Some containers heading there were previously rerouted to Korala; electric vehicles imported from China are also stranded there.

The Tatopani crossing in Sindhupalchok District has been closed from the Chinese side for about a month. Customs operations there have been suspended, although tourists are allowed to cross the border. More than 45 containers carrying ready-made garments, equipment and other goods remain in Nyalam and nearby areas of China.

Business representatives warn that prolonged restrictions could affect the supply of certain goods and prices. At the same time, Tribhuvandhar Tuladhar, president of the Nepal Trans-Himalayan Trade Association, believes that disruptions at Korala and Tatopani may be temporary, while existing stocks could limit the impact on the festival market.

China accounts for about 17% of Nepal’s imports, while it receives around 0.5% of Nepalese exports. During the first two months of the current fiscal year, Nepal imported goods worth 76.4 billion Nepalese rupees from China and exported goods worth 293.3 million rupees.

title: Nepal demands explanation for detention of former chief justice Rana — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal demands explanation for detention of former chief justice Rana — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, opposition lawmakers in both houses of parliament demanded that the government explain the detention of former chief justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana. Police detained him overnight, and the government has not provided an official explanation of the grounds for these actions, Kathmandu Post reports.

Opposition criticism

Representatives of the Nepali Congress, CPN-UML, the Communist Party of Nepal, the Nepal Workers and Peasants Party, and the Rastriya Prajatantra Party criticized the detention, calling it contrary to the rule of law. Opposition lawmakers said the authorities cited security considerations, although they could have strengthened Rana's protection rather than detaining him if threats existed.

National Assembly member Ananda Prasad Dhungana said the former chief justice was detained overnight and without a warrant. Ain Bahadur Mahar of CPN-UML said Rana was taken into custody without charges being filed and demanded an explanation of the legal basis on which he was later released.

Communist Party of Nepal lawmaker Yubaraj Dulal suggested that the overnight operation may have been an attempt to divert attention from organizing aid after natural disasters. This is the lawmaker's assumption, not an established fact. Rastriya Prajatantra Party representative Bharat Giri also said that human rights defenders were not allowed to meet Rana during his detention.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Actions by the human rights commission

Nepal's National Human Rights Commission summoned Senior Superintendent of Police Santosh Khadka, who heads the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office in Teku, to provide an explanation. The commission did so after police denied its representatives access to Rana on Sunday.

A three-member team led by commission member Manoj Duwadi arrived in Teku to verify reports that Rana was being held without a warrant. Police kept the group at the gate for 45 minutes and then did not allow it to meet the detainee.

Police said they handed Rana over to his family on Sunday afternoon to return to his residence in Bansbari. His son, Sachindra, filed an application requesting security for his father. Deputy Inspector General of Police Govinda Thapaliya said Rana was at home under police protection. At the same time, Armed Police Force personnel on duty outside his house told journalists that he had not returned home since Sunday evening.

Lawmakers from the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party did not comment on Rana's detention during parliamentary sessions. Their speeches concerned Prime Minister Balendra Shah's address to the UN General Assembly, flooding on the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, climate change, and constituency issues.

title: Nepal’s flash foods: How can communities rebuild after a disaster? - The Hindu
description: Nepal’s flash foods: How can communities rebuild after a disaster?  The Hindu
publisher.title: The Hindu
full_article:
On August 26, floods hit Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts, wiping away entire towns and communities. Roads and bridges were washed away, and telecommunications networks were down. The immediate focus was on rescuing people trapped under debris and providing relief to those affected. A month on, the focus has now shifted to rehabilitation, rebuilding and long-term recovery.

The Hindu spoke to Dr. Nimesh Dhungana, Senior Lecturer in Disaster Studies and Global Health at the University of Manchester’s Humanitarian and Conflict Response Institute (HCRI), who studies disasters through the lens of governance, democracy and accountability, about recovery after the devastating flash floods. Dr. Dhungana describes himself as an accidental disaster researcher who started studying disasters after the 2015 Nepal earthquake. He also studied the Himalayan country’s response to the COVID pandemic. Edited excerpts:

Is there a difference between the way the government responded to the 2015 earthquake, the COVID pandemic and the recent flash floods? The government has a sense of moral responsibility [to save lives] when a disaster of this scale strikes. One common element is that the state acts decisively and with the speed required in the aftermath of such disasters. It mobilises its emergency forces, led by the security forces. However, we are increasingly seeing that the state’s response is not matched by a sustained commitment to long-term recovery and reconstruction. That responsibility starts to fade, particularly when it comes to listening to affected communities and ensuring that their rights are protected during the long-term recovery and reconstruction process. It is about transparency, engagement with the affected population and ensuring that they have a say in the recovery and reconstruction process.

Your work suggests that disasters expose government failures that have built up, or existed long before the disaster itself. What do you mean by this? I think there is a long-standing debate about what constitutes a disaster. The recent floods have also forced us to revisit this basic question: what is a disaster in the first place? One way of thinking about it is as an event that is often unpredictable and attracts considerable attention from national and international media, as the recent floods did. Another way of thinking about a disaster is as a process. It is something that happens because of long-term vulnerabilities. Disasters are not caused by nature alone. It is a mixture of the two. I think there is a growing consensus that a disaster is more of a process than just an event. Unfortunately, it is more comfortable to think of a disaster as an event, something beyond our control. We saw that with the 2015 earthquake and the pandemic. This is not limited to Nepal; it is a wider issue. I think this is a problematic way of looking at disasters. It can absolve state actors of accountability. We need deeper introspection into the choices we make, our governance structures and institutions. We should adopt a more rights-based approach to disaster response and rethink how we address longstanding inequalities and injustices. The state is often quick to respond to disasters, but its approach is usually centralised and top-down. This undermines the roles and responsibilities of local bodies, which are the frontline responders.

How do you balance the role of the local bodies and the federal government, especially when a massive disaster strikes a region, leaving the local communities wiped out? It depends on the scale of the disaster. The flash floods in Nepal are unprecedented. Given the scale of the disaster, Nepal needs support from outside, not just nationally, but also internationally. However, this is no excuse for not involving local representatives in the process. Ward officials, elected representatives, local NGOs and community-based organisations, which are often at the forefront of disaster response, have greater knowledge of the local context. In the Rasuwa floods, questions have been raised about their role being undermined by the centralised, top-down disaster response. Mobilising military and security forces for disaster relief is a way of centralisation. We need to think beyond security forces for the immediate response and recovery. We need to engage more civilian actors for immediate relief and in policy-making. We should empower the local government with resources, equipment and infrastructure to deal with disasters. In the longer term, policy-wise, local bodies need to have a say in answering the big questions, like how we resettle communities. The problem is that, in Nepal and elsewhere, reconstruction tends to focus more on physical reconstruction, like building houses and other infrastructure. But they are often not aligned with community priorities. It also raises a deeper question: what does recovery mean? Is it just rebuilding houses, or is it a societal recovery? What if people don’t want to move from a certain place? How do we listen to their claims and choices? The local government can play a really important role here.

Your work says there is a difference between the community ‘having a voice’ and ‘having teeth’. What does that mean? This also stems from a more rights-based approach to thinking about development and disasters. There’s a long-standing literature on the role of voice in this kind of difficult situation, going back to Amartya Sen’s work in famine prevention. He did seminal work on how we should think about famine not just as a problem of food production, but also in terms of entitlement failures and whether communities have the right to demand answers from authorities. Be it the 2015 earthquake or the recent Rasuwa floods, bereaved families have demanded answers from the State about the way rescue and relief operations have been organised. There have also been questions about fairness and transparency in relief distribution. This is also about democracy and the responsiveness of State institutions, and whether they listen to these demands. ‘Teeth’ also means having the resources and ability to respond through concrete policy and programmatic interventions. The idea of ‘voice’ and ‘teeth’, comes from scholar Jonathan Fox’s work. I have drawn on that idea, but also looked at it in the context of disaster. Jonathan Fox talks about how ‘voice’ and ‘teeth’ come together to operate as a ‘bite’. The ‘bite’, in this sense, is concrete measures that would protect the rights and welfare of disaster-affected communities.

What should a genuinely good, decentralised, community-led approach to disaster governance look like? At the ward level, disaster management governance committees exist, but only on paper. We need human and financial resources to respond, as well as physical resources such as ambulances, hospitals and relief shelters. Emergency operations are not just about having resources; it is also about the general logic of governance. Disasters are better managed locally, as local governments have knowledge of the local context.

How do we ensure that human decisions do not make disasters even worse? This comes back to who has the power to make decisions. The major casualties of the recent Nepal floods were hydropower and the road networks. Some estimates say that almost 10% of Nepal’s hydropower infrastructure was wiped out. Who granted licenses to construct hydropower projects in these areas? This is fundamentally a question of governance. Decisions about building critical infrastructure, such as schools and hospitals, on riverbanks are linked to human choices.

Do communities that are victims of infrastructural breakdowns have any say? What role did they have in the making of these infrastructures? It is important to have a conversation about the climate crisis, but we also need to examine what happened downstream. What was the government’s role before the disaster? Did it do enough to protect the public? That is where a rights-based, more governance-centric approach to disasters comes in. It also involves a more social scientific approach to understanding disasters, rather than looking at them solely from the perspective of hazards and physical sciences.

title: Will Nepal Get Compensation From FRLD? - The Rising Nepal
description: Will Nepal Get Compensation From FRLD?  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
After the Bhotekoshi flash floods, Nepal has petitioned the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) for economic and non-economic loss sustained in the disaster. The compensation amount is USD two million. Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has argued that Nepal needs justice, not aid or charity, for the loss and property induced by the flood, a result of climate change. The blame for the disaster indirectly lies on the shoulders of the advanced countries, which greatly contribute to greenhouse gas emissions.

The FRLD is a global financing mechanism under the UN climate change framework that is designed to help climate-vulnerable poor countries to cope with the impacts of climate change, both economic and non-economic. The FRLD was established at COP 27, which was held in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, in 2022, after three decades of struggle on the part of least developed and developing countries. It was brought into operation at COP 28, held in Dubai in 2023.

Santiago Network

The parties agreed to adopt the Santiago Network, which was set up at COP 25, held in Madrid in 2019, to provide technical assistance in managing loss and damage arising out of climate-related disasters. The FRLD runs as a financial mechanism of the Paris Agreement. At previous COP events, wealthy countries thwarted attempts by poor countries to get financial assistance for climate adaptation and to cope with climate-related disasters. At COP 26, held in Glasgow, Scotland became the first Global North country to pledge bilateral finance for loss and damage. The US withdrew from the FRLD in March 2025.

The FRLD provides financial assistance for extreme weather events such as flash floods and storms and slow-onset events such as sea-level rise. The FRLD is managed by a Board of 26 members from both developed and developing nations. The World Bank acts as the interim trustee.

The FRLD is intended to help vulnerable countries cope with irreversible impacts of climate change and develop adaption plans to mitigate the impacts. The FRLD is also designed to help such countries bounce back from climate-related loss and damage. Under the operational mechanism of the FRLD, country-specific needs and priorities are accentuated with a focus on thrashing out solutions based on local and contextual conditions. Least developed and developing countries are often cash-strapped. They cannot manage funds for regular development works, let alone for disasters induced by climate change. As such, they need financial assistance for adaptation, recovery, relocation and rehabilitation plans. In fact, they need financial support so that they avert, minimise and cope with damage and risks from climate-related disasters.

Contributions to the FRLD are voluntary. There are no rules regarding how much developed and developing countries should contribute to the FRLD. Poor countries bearing the brunt of climate change impacts have requested billions of dollars to help those in need. As of mid-August 2026, wealthy countries had pledged a total of USD 822 million to the FRLD, but the actual funds ranged from USD 250 million to USD 300 million. The accumulation of contributions to the FRLD is taking place too slowly. Nepal has requested the FRLD to provide compensation of USD two million. It may be noted that as many as 119 countries have submitted 176 funding applications to the FRLD. The total compensation requested stands at USD 2.8 billion, which far exceeds the accumulated funds the FRLD has at its disposal.

At the Board meeting of the FRLD held in June 2026, four applications were deliberated on and considered for compensation, but unfortunately, none were approved. In the case of Nepal, eight out of 26 Board members requested an emergency meeting in view of Nepal’s unprecedented disaster. The co-chairs of the Board acknowledged Nepal’s request. The next Board meeting is taking place in December 2026. Whether the Board will consider Nepal’s request positively is up in the air. The compensation from the FRLD, based on the disbursement of grants capped at USD five to 20 million per project, seems to be climate justice for Nepal because there is already a deposit of over Rs. 15.50 billion, equivalent to over USD 100 million, in the Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund. Nepal needs USD four to five billion for reconstruction.

Himalayas and the Hindu Kush

The impacts of climate change are noticeably perceived in the Himalayas and the Hindu Kush. These ranges have the world’s largest volumes of ice. However, these vast volumes of ice are getting lost year after year. The rate of loss has been accelerating, especially since 2000. Greenhouse gas emissions are the major culprit behind climate change. According to the UN Environment Programme report released in September 2026, it is now inevitable that the planet will warm by at least 1.5 degrees Celsius vis-à-vis temperatures before the Industrial Revolution. The world is committed under the Paris Agreement to limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius to avoid the worst effects of climate change, but the efforts have yet to come into fruition.

The FRLD needs to be active and quick to respond to the urgent needs of climate-vulnerable countries. The intention of the FRLD will be defeated if it fails to deliver justice to climate-vulnerable countries like Nepal. For Nepal, whether its request is considered in a positive light or not could be a test of the credibility of the FRLD.





(Maharjan has been regularly writing on contemporary issues for this daily since 2000.)

title: Changed friendship - Telegraph India
description: Changed friendship  Telegraph India
publisher.title: Telegraph India
full_article:
On August 27, as Nepal grappled with the immediate aftermath of the devastating floods a day earlier, India’s foreign office spokesperson was asked a seemingly tone-deaf question at a media briefing. India had already announced early assistance to Nepal in its search and rescue efforts. What name had India decided on, for its operation, the reporter asked? The ministry of external affairs spokesperson, Randhir Jaiswal, responded by saying that the government has not decided on a name for its aid initiative yet. A month later, it still hasn’t announced any name. That may seem like an oversight for a government that loves advertising its disaster relief operations, from Venezuela to the Maldives. But it isn’t.

Instead, it’s a quiet acknowledgement of how India’s last major assistance mission in Nepal fuelled major blowback against New Delhi precisely because it was seen as a public relations campaign for the Narendra Modi government. Eleven years ago, hours after Nepal was hit by a 7.8 magnitude earthquake, India gave its aid mission even as it launched it. But Operation Maitri, to many Nepalis, was never really about maitri. It seemed to be about Modi. Modi himself claimed that the then Nepali prime minister, Sushil Koirala, who was travelling at the time, first learned of the earthquake in his own country from a tweet by Modi. Koirala never confirmed or denied the claim. But even if it were true, the Modi’s comment amounted to the public embarrassment of a neighbouring nation’s leadership.

Operation Maitri became India’s largest humanitarian assistance mission at the time. Thousands of soldiers helped rescue survivors. India rushed oxygen cylinders and earth movers, medicines and blankets. And the army deputed senior officers to oversee Indian aid efforts. But the mission came with cameras attached. An army of television reporters descended on Nepal, turning a humanitarian crisis into a prop for the narrative of a powerful, magnanimous New India. Microphones were thrust before grieving women and cameras were focused on injured children being wheeled into an operation. The pain of Nepal was forgotten, replaced by the pride of the aid-giver. Anger followed swiftly from the Nepali streets. By April 28, two days after the earthquake, social media was filled with viral hashtags asking the Indian media to go back.

Worse would follow. Later that same year, tensions rose between New Delhi and Kathmandu over Nepal’s enactment of a controversial new Constitution that the country’s Madhesi population, bordering India, viewed as discriminatory. India protested and sought a rethink in Kathmandu. Nepal refused and a blockade came into effect between India and landlocked Nepal. India has consistently insisted that the blockade was instituted by Madhesi groups. But Nepal accused New Delhi of orchestrating the border closure to pressure Kathmandu. It took years for ties to return to a semblance of normalcy.

In the meantime, the Indian government launched a series of assistance missions for countries in need, increasing its stature as a major provider of humanitarian aid amid calamity, even as its wordsmiths worked equally feverishly to conjure up names for those efforts. There had been Operation Neer for the Maldives in 2014. There was Operation Raahat in Yemen in 2015, then Mission Sagar amid Covid-19 for a range of Indian Ocean nations. There was Operation Dost after Turkey’s 2023 earthquake, and Operation Sagar Bandhu to assist Sri Lanka in December 2025 and Operation Amistad after Venezuela’s earthquake in June 2026. These rescue, relief and aid operations have highlighted the best of India’s abilities as a worthy friend.

Indeed, in Nepal, too, after the August flash floods, the Indian government was prompt and responsive in deploying personnel, technical expertise, equipment and humanitarian assistance on a scale no other country has come close to matching. But it has done so in a far more understated way than 11 years ago and, this time, without even a formal name for the assistance.

Nepal has helped India learn the difference between a friend in need and a friend who is needy of recognition. The former wins administration, the latter revulsion.

Charu Sudan Kasturi is a journalist who writes on foreign policy and international relations
